ambiguities.description: The requester of a plan change is mentioned but not clearly defined - is it a Person, an Account contact, or a User/employee? No identifier or type is given.

source_references.excerpt: It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

ambiguities.description: The commercial (business) rule for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions is explicitly undecided - should it run to term, be prorated, or generate a refund/credit? The system behavior (end date set to paid-through date, no refund) is captured, but the business policy is not resolved.

source_references.excerpt: What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: The word 'plan' is used for at least three different concepts: PricePlan (billing artefact), FeatureBundle (feature/pricing-page plan), and a sales-negotiated deal (never modeled). This is an overloaded term explicitly flagged by the participants.

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan. / We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.

ambiguities.description: 'Paused' is described as a separate boolean flag that overlaps confusingly with Status, causing bugs (paused subscriptions appear in 'active' queries). It's unclear whether Paused should be modeled as a value type/attribute, or whether it should actually be a fifth status. This constraint/overlap is not fully resolved.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. / It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: Tom notes a fourth product is 'in discovery' - it's unclear whether the Product value constraint (CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT) should be treated as closed/fixed or open-ended since a new product code may be added soon.

source_references.excerpt: Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: The relationship between Account and Company (the real-world business) is ambiguous. Tom notes that when an account closes and the company returns, a new account number is issued and treated as a new customer, losing history. It's unclear if 'Company' should be modeled as a separate concept from Account for product/history purposes, even though Priya says Company Name is not an identifier.

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting. / Which drives me mad, incidentally, because from a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history.

ambiguities.description: It's unclear whether the four manual/goodwill refund credits mentioned by Tom should be modeled as a distinct fact type (e.g., a Credit or Refund entity) since they currently exist 'outside the subscription' system with no formal mechanism.

source_references.excerpt: There's no refund mechanism at all -- the four Tom's talking about were manual credits raised outside the subscription.

ambiguities.description: Granularity: it is unclear whether Contact/Email (mentioned briefly as being on the 'contact' not the account) should be modeled as its own entity type, since no further detail was given about what a Contact is or how many an account may have.

source_references.excerpt: Company name absolutely not, we have four accounts called "Acme." Email is on the contact, not the account.

object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account; everything (subscriptions, billing) hangs off it. Treated as a new customer if it closes and reopens.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.
Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: Six-digit, sequential, never-reused identifier for an Account.

source_references.excerpt: Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a given amount on a given cycle for a given product/plan.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: PricePlan

object_types.name: PlanCode

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: The feature bundle a customer gets -- seats, API access, SSO, etc; what's shown on the pricing page.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: Date a subscription ends; optional, present only for fixed-term subscriptions or after cancellation.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The billing cycle for a subscription: monthly or annual.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change of price plan on a subscription, with who requested it and when it takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date, and the subscription's current plan is derived from the change history. / It's got a change ID.
It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
